title: Remote jobs with US and EU companies from India: tax, FEMA and GST
excerpt: Working from India for a foreign company? Compare EOR, contractor and employee routes, and the income tax, FEMA and GST rules that apply from October 2026.

content:
A US or European company can pay you for remote work from India in three ways: through its own Indian entity, through an employer of record (EOR) that employs you on its behalf, or as an independent contractor who sends invoices. Employees have tax deducted at source and get provident fund and gratuity; contractors run a small export business and handle their own income tax, GST and foreign-exchange paperwork.

That paperwork changed this month. From 1 October 2026, the Reserve Bank of India's new export and import regulations replaced its older rulebook, and an amendment dated 22 September 2026 cut the time an exporter has to bring payment into India to nine months. Contractors who bill foreign clients are service exporters under these rules. This guide explains each route and the income tax, FEMA (Foreign Exchange Management Act) and GST rules that apply. It is general information, not legal or tax advice: confirm your own case with a chartered accountant, your bank or the official sources linked below. (₹1 lakh is ₹1,00,000; LPA means lakh per annum.)

Key takeaways

  • As an employee, directly or through an EOR, you are paid a salary with tax deducted in India, and there is no GST on it.
  • As a contractor you are self-employed: you pay advance tax yourself, and the presumptive scheme can treat 50% of your receipts as profit if receipts stay within ₹75 lakh and cash is no more than 5% of them.
  • Since 1 October 2026, the full value of an export of services must be realised within nine months, or 12 months for rupee invoices.
  • GST registration is needed once aggregate turnover, including exports, crosses ₹20 lakh (₹10 lakh in special category states); a Letter of Undertaking lets you export without paying IGST.
  • The Liberalised Remittance Scheme limit of $250,000 a year covers money you send abroad, not payments you receive.

Three ways a foreign company can hire you from India

The contract you sign, not the job title, decides which rules apply. This table summarises the three common set-ups.

RouteYour legal employerWho handles income taxStatutory benefitsYour paperwork
Employee of the company's Indian entityThe Indian subsidiary or capability centreEmployer deducts tax monthlyProvident fund, gratuity and other Indian benefitsLow: annual return
Employee of an employer of recordThe EOR's Indian companyEOR deducts tax monthlyProvident fund, ESI where eligible, gratuityLow: annual return
Independent contractorNone: you are a businessYou, through advance taxNone by lawHigh: invoices, GST, export declarations, books

An EOR is a locally incorporated company that becomes your legal employer while the foreign company directs your daily work, according to Deel, which sells EOR services. Deel says the EOR signs the employment contract under Indian law, deducts tax at source every month, remits provident fund contributions and Employees' State Insurance (ESI) where it applies, and administers gratuity for staff who complete five years. It also says the arrangement lets a foreign company avoid creating a "permanent establishment" in India, which could expose it to Indian corporate tax.

Contracting is simpler for the company but carries a risk if the role looks like a job. Deel notes that Indian courts have reclassified contractors as employees and ordered back pay and benefits. If a company sets your hours, gives you its equipment and treats you like staff for years, ask whether an employment route is available.

Income tax: who pays, and on what

Residency decides where you are taxed

Under section 6 of the Income-tax Act, 2025, which replaced the 1961 Act from 1 April 2026, you are resident in India for a tax year if you spend 182 days or more in the country, or at least 60 days in the year plus 365 days over the four preceding years, according to eztax's annotated text of the Act. Section 5 then brings into a resident's income whatever is received in India, accrues in India, or accrues outside India; for a person who is "not ordinarily resident", foreign income counts only if it comes from a business controlled or a profession set up in India, according to the same source. In plain terms, if you live in India and work for a US or German company, India taxes that income.

On the other side, the US Internal Revenue Service's Publication 515 says pay for services performed outside the United States is foreign-source income, according to the IRS. So if all your work is done from India, the US treats that pay as foreign-source income. Europe has its own rules by country; check with the client and your adviser.

If you are an employee or work through an EOR

Your employer or EOR deducts tax every month, exactly as an Indian employer would, and the salary is reported in your annual return. To compare an EOR offer with an Indian offer, run both CTC (cost to company) figures through our in-hand salary calculator, which models the new and old regimes and the provident fund wage ceiling.

If you are a contractor

You are taxed as a professional. The presumptive scheme for specified professions, section 44ADA under the old Act, now sits in section 58 of the 2025 Act. It treats 50% of gross receipts as income. The limit is ₹50 lakh of receipts, raised to ₹75 lakh when cash receipts do not exceed 5% of the total, according to an analysis on TaxGuru by chartered accountant Ajay Kumar Agrawal. Payments from foreign clients arrive by bank transfer, so most remote contractors can use the higher limit. Opting in is a choice: if your real costs are higher, you can keep books and claim actual expenses instead.

Example: a developer in Pune who invoices a Berlin company ₹40 lakh in a tax year, all through her bank, can declare ₹20 lakh as income under the scheme and pay tax on that at slab rates. Because nobody deducts tax for her, she pays advance tax during the year.

FEMA: getting paid from abroad, legally

For a contractor, every invoice to a foreign client is an export of services, so foreign-exchange rules apply. The RBI's Foreign Exchange Management (Export and Import of Goods and Services) Regulations, 2026, dated 13 January 2026, took effect on 1 October 2026 and supersede the 2015 master direction on exports and 167 older circulars, according to law firm AZB & Partners.

The deadline to bring the money home moved twice this year. The original 2026 regulations allowed 15 months. The RBI's amendment notification of 22 September 2026 substitutes "nine months" for "fifteen months", and 12 months for 18 months where exports are invoiced or settled in rupees, with effect from 1 October 2026, according to the RBI notification.

Service exporters also file an export declaration form (EDF) for the full export value. Taxmann's summary of the regulations says the declaration is generally due within 30 days from the end of the month in which the invoice is raised, that one consolidated form can cover a month's exports, and that the authorised dealer bank can extend the deadline, according to Taxmann. Ask your bank how it wants these filed, and keep its inward remittance advice for every payment.

Where LRS fits

The Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS) is for money going out of India. It lets a resident individual remit up to $250,000 in a financial year for permitted purposes, according to the RBI's LRS FAQs, which also say no prior approval is needed to open a foreign currency account with a bank abroad to make LRS remittances, and that investments made abroad must follow the Overseas Investment Rules and Regulations, 2022. Your incoming salary or fees are not LRS transactions. LRS matters when you use your earnings to invest abroad, for example in a foreign brokerage account.

GST on export of services, and the LUT

Employees can skip this section. Services by an employee to an employer in the course of employment are listed in Schedule III of the CGST Act as neither a supply of goods nor of services, according to TaxGuru, so there is no GST on salary, whether it comes from a subsidiary or an EOR.

Contractors need to check two things.

1. Does your work count as an export?

Section 2(6) of the IGST Act sets five conditions that must all hold: you are located in India, the client is outside India, the place of supply is outside India, payment comes in convertible foreign exchange or in rupees where the RBI allows it, and you and the client are not merely establishments of the same person, according to a TaxGuru explainer from Compliance Calendar LLP. The same piece warns that an intermediary, someone who arranges services between two other parties, is generally treated as supplying where the supplier is located, so a pure middle-man role may fail the test. Exports that qualify are zero-rated rather than exempt, which lets you keep input tax credit.

2. Do you need to register and file a LUT?

You do not need GST registration until aggregate turnover passes ₹20 lakh in a year, or ₹10 lakh in special category states, and export receipts count towards that figure, according to TaxAdda. Once registered, file a Letter of Undertaking (LUT) in form GST RFD-11 on the GST portal before you export, so you can invoice without charging integrated GST (IGST). The GST portal's help pages say a LUT is valid for one financial year and then expires, must be signed by an authorised signatory, and is not available to anyone prosecuted for tax evasion of ₹2.5 crore or more, according to the GST portal. Without a LUT you can still export by paying IGST and claiming a refund later.

One timing detail matters. Under rule 96A of the GST rules, a LUT exporter undertakes to receive payment within one year of the invoice, unless the commissioner allows longer, according to the TaxGuru explainer. FEMA's nine-month limit is now the tighter of the two, so plan around nine months.

A worked comparison: two offers for the same role

Say a London fintech offers a backend engineer in Bengaluru two options: ₹36 lakh a year as an EOR employee, or ₹42 lakh a year invoiced as a contractor. The figures are illustrative.

  • EOR offer. The EOR deducts tax monthly and contributes to provident fund, and gratuity builds up after five years. There is no GST or export filing. Enter ₹36 lakh in the in-hand calculator to see the monthly take-home.
  • Contract offer. Under section 58, ₹21 lakh (half of ₹42 lakh) is treated as income, taxed at slab rates through advance tax. Turnover is above ₹20 lakh, so GST registration and a yearly LUT are needed, plus an export declaration for each month's invoices and payment within nine months. There is no employer provident fund, gratuity or group health cover, so budget for those yourself.

The contract pays more on paper and may leave more in hand after tax. Against that, you lose benefits and job protection and take on hours of compliance. Price both before you choose.

Checklist before you sign

  • Ask which route the role uses and who your legal employer will be. If an EOR, ask for its name and a sample payslip.
  • For contracts: confirm the client is outside India, the currency of payment, payment terms within nine months, and that your work is not an intermediary role.
  • Register for GST before you cross ₹20 lakh and file the LUT at the start of every financial year.
  • Keep a bank inward remittance advice for every payment and match it to an invoice.
  • Set aside advance tax each quarter and keep a simple ledger even if you use the presumptive scheme.

Bottom line

For a long-term full-time role, employment through the company's entity or an EOR is the cleaner choice: benefits, deducted tax and no export paperwork. Contracting suits people with several clients or short projects who are ready to run a business, and the new nine-month FEMA deadline from 1 October 2026 means chasing late invoices is now part of the job. Browse current remote jobs or the full jobs board to see which companies hire from India.

FAQ

Do I pay tax in both India and the US on remote work?

If you are an Indian resident working only from India, the income is taxed in India; the IRS treats pay for work performed outside the US as foreign-source income.

Is an employer of record better than a contract?

For a full-time, long-term role usually yes: the EOR handles tax deduction, provident fund and gratuity. A contract can pay more but shifts tax, GST and FEMA work to you.

Do freelancers have to charge GST to foreign clients?

Not if the work qualifies as an export and you have filed a LUT. Below ₹20 lakh of aggregate turnover you do not need GST registration at all.

How long can I wait to receive a foreign payment?

From 1 October 2026, nine months under the RBI's export regulations, or 12 months for exports invoiced or settled in rupees.

Does receiving dollars count against my LRS limit?

No. LRS covers remittances out of India, capped at $250,000 a financial year.
